Efface

/ih-FAYSS/ - rhymes with place · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Efface means to wipe out or rub away.

Generations of pilgrims' fingertips have begun to efface the bronze lion's mane, polishing the curls into smooth bright metal.

Worked Example

The letters on the lab's oldest keyboard have been effaced by a million keystrokes — E, A and S are bare black squares now, and visitors type by memory or not at all.

Efface is more precise than remove or destroy because it means wearing a mark off a surface little by little — rubbing, friction, and use doing quietly what no single act did.

How Efface Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

erase

erase: remove deliberately, usually in one act

abrade

abrade: scrape a surface away by friction — strictly physical

Antonyms

engrave

engrave: cut a mark in deep so that it lasts

preserve

preserve: guard something from wear and loss

How Strong Is It? — dim → fade → efface

dim vs. efface

dim vs. efface: Dim is the gentlest change — the mark merely loses brightness and is still plainly there.

fade vs. efface

fade vs. efface: Fade is stronger than dim but still stops short of efface: a faded mark survives as a ghost, while an effaced one is gone from the surface altogether.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of efface.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ef-

Prefix — ef-: out, away (the form ex- takes before f)

Root — face

Root — face: face, surface (Latin facies)

Put it together

Put it together: Ef- (out, away — the shape ex- takes before an f) + face (Latin facies, the face or surface) = to take the face off a thing: to work its surface away until the mark is gone. The root is everywhere — a building's facade is its street face, and surface itself carries it. Efface keeps the physical picture: wear, weather and rubbing, grain by grain.

Use the root in a new word: facade

Use the root in a new word: facade: Ivy had climbed the facade so thickly that only the doorway still showed the original brick.

Root Check

Word Choice

literary / precise

Efface is precise and a little literary: it names gradual removal from a surface — wear, weather, rubbing, grain by grain. Erase is the everyday deliberate act, and expunge, taught in this unit, is the official word for wiping an entry from a record rather than a mark from a surface. People can also efface themselves: self-effacing means keeping quietly to the background.
